scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

Community celebrations are about *togetherness*, not about one family carrying the entire burden. Here’s how to navigate this thoughtfully and compassionately: --- ### ✨ **Key Truths to Remember:** - **"Enough for the whole community" is almost never literal** — no single family is expected to feed hundreds of people. This is likely a misunderstanding or an outdated expectation. - **True community spirit is about shared effort** — not one family doing all the work while others contribute nothing. - **Your family’s well-being comes first**. If you overspending now would cause stress, debt, or hunger for *your own household*, that’s not sustainable or healthy. - **You can still participate meaningfully without breaking the bank**. In fact, *honesty and boundaries* often strengthen community trust. --- ### 🌱 **Practical, Budget-Friendly Solutions:** 1. **Talk to your mom (and others) about realistic expectations:** - * " Mom, I love that we want to contribute, but our budget is tight right now. I’m happy to bring a dish we *can* afford, but I don’t want to overspending and stress our family. Can we ask others to bring something too? Maybe we can all share the load?"* - * " I heard the event is for 50 people — would it help if I brought 10 servings instead of 50? That way I’m still contributing, but it’s manageable for us."* 2. **Contribute in non-food ways ( often equally valued!):** - Offer to help set up chairs, clean up afterward, or organize games. - Bring a simple, *low-cost* dish (e.g., a homemade bread, a tray of fruit, or a shared salad you can make in bulk for $5–$10). - * " I’m short on funds right now, but I’d love to volunteer to help with setup or cleanup — that way I can still be part of the celebration without straining our budget."* 3. **Collaborate with neighbors or other families:** - * " I’m bringing a big pot of soup — would anyone else like to join me? We could split the cost and make it a 'community soup pot'!"* - Many communities have a " potluck where everyone brings a dish to share — **this is normal and expected**. If your family is the only one expected to feed everyone, that’s not a healthy dynamic. 4. **If it’s a " donation-based" event (e.g., a fundraiser):** - * " I’d love to donate $X to the event fund instead of bringing food — that way I can support it without overspending on groceries."* - (Many events *prefer* cash donations over food, as it’s easier to manage.) --- ### 💬 **Why This Works:** - **It’s honest and respectful** — people appreciate transparency. - **It models healthy boundaries** — your family’s stability matters. - **It shifts the focus to *togetherness***, not just food. - **Most communities will understand** — especially if you’re willing to contribute *something* (time, a small dish, or a donation). > ** real community doesn’t ask you to sacrifice your family’s well-being.** > — If someone *does* pressure you to overspending, that’s not true community spirit — it’s a red flag. --- ### 🌟 **Final Thought:** You’re already showing care by wanting to contribute. **That’s what matters most.** A small, heartfelt gesture ( like a shared dish, a helping hand, or a kind word) means far more than a financially ruinous effort. **You’re not " letting the community down" — you’re being responsible.** And that’s something to be proud of. 💛 Would you like help brainstorming a specific low-cost dish or script for talking to your mom?
